segments.title: Introduction to Big O Notation in Computer Science

sub_topics.name: Introduction to the Video
sub_topics.description: Hey, what's going on everybody? It's your bro, hope you're doing well, and in this video I'm going to describe the very basics of Big O notation in, well, computer science.

sub_topics.name: What is Big O Notation
sub_topics.description: Oh yeah, Big O notation. So a common phrase used with Big O notation is, how code slows as data grows. It describes the performance of an algorithm as the amount of data increases. And really, this notation is machine independent. What we're really focusing on is the number of steps to complete an algorithm, because some machines are going to run certain algorithms faster than others.

key_points: Big O notation is used to describe the performance of an algorithm
It focuses on the number of steps to complete an algorithm

segments.title: Examples of Big O Notation in Practice

sub_topics.name: Example of a Function with O(n) Runtime Complexity
sub_topics.description: Here's a more concrete example. I have a function named addup. We will add up to a certain number depending on what we pass in as an argument. The for loop within here will iterate once up to whatever number that n is, add i to sum, then return it.

sub_topics.name: Example of a Function with O(1) Runtime Complexity
sub_topics.description: Now another way which we could write the same function is to take sum equals n times n plus 1 divided by 2. We will get the exact same sum. So if n was, let's say, a million, this is still only going to take a couple seconds. steps. Three steps, not a million steps.

key_points: O(n) runtime complexity means the algorithm takes linear time
O(1) runtime complexity means the algorithm takes constant time
The input size does not affect the runtime complexity of an O(1) algorithm

sub_topics.name: Graphical Representation of Runtime Complexities
sub_topics.description: Here's a graph that I made to represent the different runtime complexities. We have data on the x-axis represented by n. So data will increase as we go more to the right, and we have time on the y-axis.

sub_topics.name: Explanation of Different Runtime Complexities
sub_topics.description: So let begin with O of 1 constant time. Anything that has a runtime complexity of O of 1 will take the same amount of time regardless of the data size. A few examples would include the random access of an element within an array and inserting at the beginning of a linked list.
